chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
name: Production Across Countries: What Is an MNC?

scenes.animation: Zippy opens a new gadget box. Tiny flags pop out of each part: the design booklet shows the USA, a circuit board shows China, the assembled body shows Mexico, and a helpline card shows India. Zippy spins around, dizzy.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Designed in one country, parts from another, assembled somewhere else, helpline in India. Which country made this thing?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: All of them. Welcome to the world of multinational corporations.

scenes.animation: A definition card appears: 'MNC: a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation'. A globe spins, with factory and office icons popping up in many countries, all connected by lines to one headquarters.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A multinational corporation, or MNC, is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: MNCs set up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources. This is done so that the cost of production is low, and the MNCs can earn greater profits.

scenes.animation: A world map. A flowchart traces a large MNC producing industrial equipment: 'Design: research centres in the United States' → 'Components: China' → 'Assembly: Mexico and Eastern Europe' → 'Sold all over the world', with a headset icon over India labelled 'Customer care through call centres'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Take a large MNC producing industrial equipment. It designs its products in research centres in the United States. Components are manufactured in China, then shipped to Mexico and Eastern Europe, where the products are assembled.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The finished products are sold all over the world. Meanwhile, customer care is carried out through call centres located in India.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So production is spread across the globe like a relay race!

scenes.animation: A checklist appears above a map of India: 'Close to markets', 'Skilled and unskilled labour at low cost', 'Availability of other factors of production', 'Government policies that look after their interests'. Each item ticks off.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: How does an MNC choose where to set up production? It looks for places close to markets, with skilled and unskilled labour available at low costs, and where other factors of production are assured.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It also looks for government policies that look after its interests.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The money that MNCs spend to buy assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment is called investment. Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment.

scenes.animation: A board-tip card appears with the definition of MNC highlighted in yellow and the word 'foreign investment' circled.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: learn the exact definition of an MNC and the factors that decide where it sets up production. Both are frequent questions.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a globe icon. Points appear: '1. MNC = owns or controls production in more than one nation', '2. Production spread across countries to cut costs', '3. MNC investment = foreign investment'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: an MNC owns or controls production in more than one nation.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: MNCs spread production across countries where costs are low, to earn greater profits.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My gadget is officially a world citizen.

chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
name: Interlinking Production and Foreign Trade

scenes.animation: A toy shop during Diwali. Rows of colourful Chinese toys with low price tags crowd the shelves. An Indian toy maker stands beside his shelf, looking worried as customers walk past.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: These toys are cheaper and cooler. Everyone's buying them!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's foreign trade at work. But first, let's see how MNCs link up with local producers.

scenes.animation: Three doorways appear, each labelled. Door 1 'Joint production with local companies': an MNC hands money and machines to an Indian factory. Door 2 'Buying up local companies': a big MNC swallows a smaller company logo. Door 3 'Placing orders with small producers': MNC orders sheets fly to small workshops making garments, footwear and sports items.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: MNCs interlink production in different ways. Sometimes they set up production jointly with local companies. The MNC provides money for additional investments and the latest technology.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The most common route is to buy up local companies and then expand production. Cargill Foods, a very large American MNC, bought over smaller Indian companies such as Parakh Foods. Cargill is now the largest producer of edible oil in India.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Large MNCs also place orders with small producers. Garments, footwear and sports items are examples of industries where production is carried out by many small producers around the world.

scenes.animation: A world map. Ships cross between China and India carrying toys one way and other goods the other way. A caption reads 'Foreign trade = connecting markets across countries'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Foreign trade creates an opportunity for producers to reach beyond the markets of their own countries. Buyers get a choice of goods beyond what is produced domestically.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: When Chinese toys come into Indian markets, buyers get more choice at lower prices. But Indian toy makers face losses as their toys are not bought as much.

scenes.animation: Two market bubbles, 'India' and 'China', slowly merge into one. The prices of toys on both sides move closer together. A label reads 'Integration of markets'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So trade joins markets together?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Foreign trade results in connecting the markets, or integration of markets, in different countries. Prices of similar goods in the two markets tend to become equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: remember the three ways MNCs interlink production, with the Cargill example.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a link-chain icon. Points appear: '1. Joint production, buying local companies, placing orders', '2. Cargill bought Parakh Foods', '3. Foreign trade integrates markets'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: MNCs interlink production through joint production, buying local companies, and placing orders with small producers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Cargill Foods bought Parakh Foods and became the largest producer of edible oil in India.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: foreign trade connects and integrates markets across countries.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'll buy one Indian toy and one Chinese toy. Fair and balanced.

chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
name: What Is Globalisation? Technology and Liberalisation

scenes.animation: An office in London. An editor clicks 'Send' on a laptop. A glowing email zips across the globe into a design studio in Delhi, where the magazine is designed and printed. Zippy watches it fly past his face.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A magazine for London readers, designed and printed in Delhi? How?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Through technology and open policies. Together, they drive globalisation.

scenes.animation: A globe with arrows criss-crossing between countries, labelled 'Goods', 'Services', 'Investment', 'Technology', 'People'. The 'People' arrow is thinner than the rest. The title reads 'Globalisation = rapid integration or interconnection between countries'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. More and more goods and services, investments and technology are moving between countries.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: There is also some movement of people between countries, mostly in search of better income, jobs or education. But this has been limited.

scenes.animation: A container ship loaded with metal containers glides across the sea, then a jet plane. Next, satellites, mobile phones, computers and the internet link up. Label: 'Rapid improvement in technology'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The first factor is rapid improvement in technology. Transportation technology has improved, making delivery of goods over long distances faster and cheaper, for example using containers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Even more important is information and communication technology. Telecommunication facilities, computers and the internet let people across the world contact each other instantly and share information.

scenes.animation: A border gate labelled 'Trade barrier: tax on imports' blocks trucks of foreign goods. The year stamp 'After Independence' shows the barrier up. Then a stamp '1991' appears, and the gate lifts. Label: 'Liberalisation = removing barriers set by government'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The second factor is liberalisation of foreign trade and investment policy. A tax on imports is an example of a trade barrier. The government can use it to decide how much foreign trade is allowed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After Independence, the Indian government put barriers on foreign trade and investment to protect producers in the country from foreign competition.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Starting around 1991, some far-reaching changes were made. Barriers were removed to a large extent. Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is called liberalisation.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the gate opened, and the world walked in.

scenes.animation: A board-tip card: 'Factors enabling globalisation: 1. Technology 2. Liberalisation'. The year 1991 is circled in red.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: examiners love asking for the factors that enabled globalisation. Name technology and liberalisation, with examples.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the globe and a lifting gate icon. Points appear: '1. Globalisation = rapid integration between countries', '2. Technology: transport, IT', '3. Liberalisation from around 1991'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: globalisation is the rapid integration or interconnection between countries.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: technology in transport and information made it possible.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: liberalisation from around 1991 removed trade and investment barriers in India.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Email sent. Magazine printed. World connected.

chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
name: WTO and the Impact of Globalisation in India

scenes.animation: A referee in a striped shirt labelled 'WTO' blows a whistle at a trade football match between 'Developed countries' and 'Developing countries'. The developed team secretly keeps a wall of barriers near their own goal.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Who makes the rules for trade between countries?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The World Trade Organisation. But whether the rules are applied fairly is another question.

scenes.animation: A WTO building with a banner 'Aim: liberalise international trade'. A rulebook opens. Then a US farm appears with bags of money labelled 'Government support' flowing to farmers, while an Indian farmer stands with an empty hand.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The World Trade Organisation aims to liberalise international trade. It was started at the initiative of developed countries, and it establishes rules regarding international trade.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Though WTO rules have forced developing countries to remove trade barriers, developed countries have unfairly retained them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For example, the US government gives massive sums of money to its farmers, so they can sell farm products at abnormally low prices. Developing countries are asked to stop supporting their farmers.

scenes.animation: A well-off urban family in a showroom picking between many brands of phones, cars and televisions. Labels read 'Greater choice', 'Improved quality', 'Lower prices'. Then factories open with signs: 'MNC investment: cellphones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food, banking'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now the impact on India. Globalisation has benefited consumers, particularly the well-off sections in urban areas. There is greater choice, with improved quality and lower prices for several products.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: MNCs have increased their investments in India, in industries like cellphones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and banking. New jobs have been created, and local companies supplying raw materials have prospered.

scenes.animation: Five Indian company logos rise onto a world stage with their products: 'Tata Motors: automobiles', 'Infosys: IT', 'Ranbaxy: medicines', 'Asian Paints: paints', 'Sundaram Fasteners: nuts and bolts'. A banner reads 'Indian companies become MNCs'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Did Indian companies benefit too?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Several top Indian companies benefited from the new competition. They invested in newer technology and raised their standards.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Some, like Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints and Sundaram Fasteners, have themselves emerged as multinationals. Globalisation also created new opportunities for companies providing services, especially in IT.

scenes.animation: A gated industrial zone labelled 'Special Economic Zone' builds with roads, power lines and offices. A tag reads 'No taxes for an initial period of five years'. A board-tip card slides in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: To attract foreign investment, governments set up Special Economic Zones with world-class facilities. Companies setting up there do not have to pay taxes for an initial period of five years.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: list Indian MNCs with their products. It's a quick-scoring question.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the WTO whistle and a rising graph. Points appear: '1. WTO liberalises trade, but developed countries retain barriers', '2. Consumers and MNC investment benefited', '3. Indian companies became MNCs; SEZs attract investment'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: the WTO aims to liberalise trade, but developed countries have unfairly retained barriers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: well-off consumers gained choice and quality, and MNC investment grew.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: some Indian companies became MNCs, and SEZs attract foreign investment.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Referee, please check the barrier wall near their goal!

chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
name: Small Producers, Uncertain Jobs and Fair Globalisation

scenes.animation: A small capacitor workshop in an industrial town. Cheap imported capacitors pile up at the gate. Workers leave one by one; the owner turns off the lights. Zippy stands in the doorway, stunned.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Wait. Globalisation was supposed to be good news. Why is this factory closing?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because its benefits have not been shared equally. For many small producers and workers, it brought great challenges.

scenes.animation: A row of products shakes under a storm cloud labelled 'Rising competition': batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, vegetable oil. Some shelves collapse and a label reads 'Units shut down, workers jobless'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For a large number of small producers and workers, globalisation has posed major challenges. Batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil are some industries where small manufacturers have been hit hard by competition.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Several units have shut down, rendering many workers jobless.

scenes.animation: A garment factory. A big MNC buyer demands 'Lowest price, best quality, delivered on time'. The factory owner turns to workers: permanent contracts are torn up and replaced with 'Temporary' tags. Clocks show long hours and night shifts.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Competition has also changed the lives of workers. Faced with growing competition, most employers now prefer to employ workers flexibly. Jobs are no longer secure.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Large MNCs in the garment industry demand the lowest price and top quality. To cut labour costs, exporters hire workers on a temporary basis, so they do not have to pay them for the whole year.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the workers pay the price for cheap clothes?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In many cases, yes. Workers face long working hours and night shifts during peak seasons, without the benefits they once had.

scenes.animation: A balance scale labelled 'Fair globalisation'. Weights drop onto the side of workers and small producers: 'Proper implementation of labour laws', 'Support small producers to compete', 'Trade and investment barriers if necessary', 'Negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules', 'People's organisations and campaigns'. The scale balances.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all, and ensure that its benefits are better shared.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The government can ensure that labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights. It can support small producers to improve performance until they become strong enough to compete. If necessary, it can use trade and investment barriers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It can negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules, and align with other developing countries against the domination of developed countries. People's organisations have also influenced important decisions on trade and investment.

scenes.animation: A board-tip card: 'Fair globalisation: role of government + people'. A pen underlines 'labour laws' and 'WTO negotiations'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: a five-mark question often asks how the government can ensure fair globalisation. Give at least four measures.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the balanced scale. Points appear: '1. Small producers hit by competition', '2. Workers face insecure, flexible jobs', '3. Fair globalisation: labour laws, support, WTO negotiation'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: small producers in many industries have been hit hard by competition.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: workers increasingly face flexible, insecure jobs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: fair globalisation needs labour laws, support for small producers and fairer WTO rules.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Global, yes. Unfair, no.
